overview: Valdivia names an archaeological tradition of coastal Ecuador, including villages such as Real Alto. Farming, fishing, craft work and public ceremonies connected communities over many centuries. The map’s broad outline is a cultural approximation, not evidence of a single territorial kingdom.

periods.title: Early villages
periods.summary: Households established settlements and developed pottery traditions.

periods.title: Growing community centres
periods.summary: Larger houses and public gathering places changed village life.

periods.title: Changing settlement patterns
periods.summary: People increasingly occupied surrounding settlements while older centres retained ritual roles.

items.text: Early Real Alto had small elliptical houses, probably roofed with thatch or palm leaves. Cooking and tool-making often happened outside. The useful part of a home extended beyond its walls into a busy household yard.

Later residences were larger and sturdier, with upright posts, daubed walls and broad thatched roofs. Archaeologists interpret them as homes for extended families. A bigger house could bring several generations and many daily tasks under one roof.

Microscopic remains can reveal meals that vanished thousands of years ago. At Loma Alta, researchers studied starch trapped in charred cooking-pot residues and directly dated the residue. Maize, jack beans and chilli peppers helped reconstruct food preparation.

The Loma Alta study also identified sophisticated processing of jack beans, which otherwise contain harmful substances. That makes the kitchen evidence more than a shopping list: cooks knew techniques that turned difficult ingredients into usable food.

Real Alto’s plant evidence includes cotton as well as food crops. Other identified plants supplied timber and fuel. The surrounding landscape was a store of many different materials, and knowing which plant suited which job was practical knowledge.

The region’s seasonal water required care. Archaeologists trace early rainwater-catching earthworks called albarradas to Valdivia and later traditions. They collected runoff and helped recharge groundwater; the many surviving structures belong to different periods, not one ancient building campaign.

Some Valdivia figurines are only a few centimetres tall, yet their makers carefully distinguished hairstyles. Faces could be made with a few incised lines. A tiny clay head could carry a surprising amount of personality.

Figurines were individually modelled, sometimes polished or covered with red slip. Scholars suggest links with fertility, agriculture or rain ceremonies. These are interpretations of objects and their contexts; the figures do not come with ancient explanatory labels.

Shells could become tools. At Real Alto, archaeologists found implements made from the central columns of large marine snails, alongside stone axes. Researchers connect these tools with clearing and working small plots near households.

Household finds suggest varied craft work: some contained weaving equipment, others pottery tools or materials for shell fishhooks and ornaments. Skills were distributed through the village, so neighbours could depend on one another’s workmanship.

Public mounds supported buildings associated with feasting and the treatment of the dead. Rebuilding and replastering gathering places took shared labour. Ceremonies and communal meals helped make the village a place that people returned to.

Decorated pots include recognisable plants such as maize, but these pictures do not provide a securely deciphered Valdivia sentence. No readable language sample is known for this tradition. Its surviving designs can be described without inventing words for their makers.

ending.text: Real Alto lost its earlier predominance as settlements changed and later Valdivia pottery spread. This was a long regional transformation, not a documented single conquest in 1500 BCE. Archaeological labels changed; the people and their descendants were not erased by a map endpoint.
